title: Being Heard Isn’t the Same as Being Understood
html:
Good morning,

“When all other means of communication fail, try words.”

We’re surrounded by ways to communicate. But are we getting any better at understanding each other?

We send messages, leave comments and react with emojis. We can reach someone on the other side of the world in seconds, yet struggle to explain what we mean to the person sitting beside us.

Sometimes we expect people to know what we’re thinking. Other times we fire off a reply and assume they’ll read it in the tone we intended.

Then we’re surprised when they take it the wrong way!

You’ve probably been on both sides of that.

You’ve sent something you thought was perfectly clear. And you’ve read something that left you wondering, “What’s that supposed to mean?”

Without a voice, a facial expression or a little context, there’s plenty of room for misunderstanding.

People think communication is about getting their message across.

But being heard isn’t the same as being understood.

That takes a little more effort.

It means thinking about the person receiving your words. What do they already know? What might they need you to explain? Are you giving them a chance to respond?

It also means being willing to ask, “Have I understood you properly?”

Especially when you’re certain you have.

It’s easy to start preparing your reply while someone is still talking. You hear something you disagree with and begin building your case.

Meanwhile, they’re still trying to explain.

A little patience could save you both a lot of frustration.

So could a few thoughtful words.

Think about a time someone told you they appreciated you. They probably didn’t deliver a speech. They said something simple and specific that let you know you mattered.

You might still remember it years later. Maybe even from childhood.

The same can happen with a careless remark. Something said in frustration can stay with someone long after you’ve forgotten saying it.

We don’t always get our words right.

But we can pause before we speak. Read the message again before we send it. Pick up the phone when a string of texts is making things worse.

We can say sorry without adding an excuse.

Ask for help without expecting someone to notice we need it.

Explain what’s bothering us before frustration turns into resentment.

We have plenty of ways to communicate.

Let’s give a little more thought to what we’re saying, and whether we’re making the effort to understand each other.

This Week’s Motivator

Words are powerful.

Choose them carefully. Use them wisely.

Give someone a few worth remembering.

Prompt for the Week

What have you left unsaid that someone needs to hear?

A thank you. An apology. Something you need to explain. A question you’ve been meaning to ask.

This week, find the words and make time for the conversation.

To your success!

Glenn
